one_liner: Micron's embedded C key-value engine for NVMe SSDs; its own YCSB run shows about 8x RocksDB's load throughput.
what_it_does: An embeddable, Linux-only C library that keeps a KVDB (one or more named KVSs, each roughly a table or column family) on SSDs and optional persistent memory. It offers put, get, delete, prefix deletes, prefix-filtered cursors, and snapshot-isolation transactions that span KVSs. The API is its own (hse_kvdb_*/hse_kvs_* handles that return hse_err_t), not a RocksDB-compatible drop-in. Since 2.0 it stores data as files in XFS or ext4 directories grouped into capacity, staging and pmem media classes; the 1.x release that was benchmarked needed the mpool kernel module instead.
how_it_is_fast: Writes go into c0, an in-memory layer of RCU-protected Bonsai trees split into up to 32 hash-sharded c0_kvsets, and ingest then moves them into a shallow cN tree whose root node spills into key-range leaf nodes. Each on-media kvset keeps keys (kblocks with a 'wants to be a B-tree' index and Bloom filters) apart from values (vblocks), so k-compaction rewrites only keys and node split and join change only metadata; that key-value separation is the likely source of the up-to-85% fewer bytes written than RocksDB's leveled compaction. A scheduler driven by space amplification (sp3) uses HyperLogLog garbage estimates to decide when to spill or compact, and ingest throttling keeps tail latency down. Media-class policies can also pin keys to fast storage while values tier down to cheaper SSDs.
when_to_use: Insert- or update-heavy ingest of billions of roughly 1 KB records onto local NVMe when the dataset is several times DRAM (the benchmark put 2 TB on a 256 GB host) and load time or SSD write volume is the bottleneck.

Data with natural key prefixes, such as per-tenant, per-device or time-epoch keys. A KVS created with a matching prefix.length gives you prefix-filtered cursors and single-call prefix deletes for bulk expiry.
Tiered SSD setups: set mclass.policy=staging_max_capacity to keep keys and the journal on TLC or pmem and move values to QLC, cutting writes to the low-endurance drives.
Embedded C or C++ services on x86-64 (or s390x) Linux that need atomic, snapshot-isolated transactions across several KVSs and can accept an asynchronous durability window.
when_not_to_use: You need RocksDB's API or feature set. There is no compatibility layer, the public API has no merge operator, WriteBatch, MultiGet, arbitrary range delete or backup engine, and the issue asking for backup/restore options (#4) is still open.

You need an engine someone maintains. The last master commit was 2023-08-17 and the last release was 3.0.0 in November 2022. Reported bugs (#630, #631) sit unfixed, and each major version (1 to 2 to 3) changed the storage format, so data had to be dumped and reloaded.

Non-Linux targets, HDDs or small machines. The docs support only Linux on x86_64 or s390x, SSD volumes only, a filesystem with O_DIRECT and fallocate punch-hole support, and recommend 32 GB of RAM or more.
One process needs several databases, or items exceed the hard limits: only one KVDB can be open per process, values are capped at 1 MiB and keys at about 1.3 KB.
You need each write to be durable when it returns. Commits are asynchronous, and by default the journal is flushed every 100 ms (durability.interval_ms) unless you call hse_kvdb_sync().

integration.form: shared lib (libhse-3, built from source with Meson; Meson can also build it static)
integration.dependencies: userspace-rcu, libbsd, libevent, lz4 and cJSON (lz4 and cJSON are built in as Meson subprojects by default), xxHash; libcurl for the CLI and tools only; libpmem (optional, for pmem on x86)
integration.min_toolchain: C (gnu11), Meson >= 0.63.0; minimum compiler versions not documented
integration.platforms: 64-bit Linux on x86-64 or s390x (other architectures compile through generic fallbacks but are not listed as supported); tested on RHEL 8/9, Ubuntu 18.04 to 22.04 and Fedora 35/36; storage must be SSD or pmem on XFS/ext4 (DAX for pmem)
integration.thread_safety: Data-path calls (put, get, delete, prefix delete, sync, cursor create) are thread-safe. Setup and teardown calls (hse_init, KVDB and KVS close, mclass reconfigure) are not. Each cursor, and each transaction, may be used by only one thread at a time. Only one KVDB can be open per process.

gotchas: Puts are throttled when the engine starts and self-tune over roughly 200 seconds (issue #9), which badly skews short benchmarks. Profile the storage with `hse storage profile` and set throttling.init_policy. Under load, the put path adds short sleeps unless you pass HSE_KVS_PUT_PRIO.

A KVS opened with transactions.enabled=true rejects non-transactional updates, and a KVS opened with it false rejects transactions. Prefix deletes need a filter exactly equal to the prefix.length fixed at KVS creation.

Deletes and updates do not free space right away. k-compaction leaves values that are no longer referenced inside vblocks, and garbage from prefix tombstones is not counted in the space-amplification estimate (docs/space-amp.md).

By default each process starts a REST server on a UNIX socket (rest.enabled=true), and error codes are hse_err_t, not errno. Use hse_strerror() or hse_err_to_errno(), because strerror() gives meaningless results.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Over SplinterDB, which makes a similar NVMe insert claim (6-10x RocksDB), pick HSE when you want its cross-KVS snapshot-isolation transactions, prefix deletes and multi-tier media placement. If you need the RocksDB API itself, or active upkeep, Speedb or ToplingDB is the drop-in route.
verified_claims_summary: In Micron's own v1 docs (YCSB 0.17.0, 2 billion 1,000-byte records, 96 client threads, a 2-socket Xeon E5-2690 v4 with 256 GB DRAM, four Micron 9300 NVMe drives striped with LVM, RHEL 8.1), HSE 1.7.0 from the mpool kernel-module era loaded at 986K inserts/s against 123K for RocksDB 6.6.4 (about 8x, 34 vs 271 minutes, p99.9 of 1.6 vs 19.5 ms), and run-phase gains of 'up to nearly 6x' on workloads A-D appear only as charts. RocksDB tuning, compiler and flags are not stated, the current 3.x storage layout was never re-measured, and no independent reproduction was found.
status_note: Abandoned since its last commit on 2023-08-17 (last release 3.0.0, Nov 2022); the Apache-2.0 OR MIT license makes it forkable, but it is a large Linux-only C engine rather than something to vendor lightly, and the benchmarked 1.x line depended on the mpool kernel module, whose repo (mpool-kmod) is now archived.
